title: Specific heat capacity
examples: What is the difference between specific heat capacity and latent heat?
Can you explain how we measure specific heat capacity in a lab?
If I change the material, does the heat energy change?

explain.say: Today we are learning about specific heat capacity.

items: Units are Joules per kilogram per degree Celsius

explain.say: The formula relating heat energy, mass, and temperature change is important. It is Q equals mass times specific heat times change in temperature.
A concrete example is heating one kilogram of water. If you add energy, the temperature will rise according to this formula.
In a required practical, we often use a calorimeter to measure this value accurately. We measure the heat lost by hot water to cooler water.
If we know the energy and the mass, we can find the specific heat capacity. We rearrange the formula to solve for c.
In everyday life, this concept explains why water is so good at keeping things warm. It takes a lot of energy to change its temperature.

faq.q: What is the difference between specific heat capacity and thermal energy?
faq.a: Specific heat capacity is a property of a substance itself. Thermal energy is the total amount of energy needed to change the substance's temperature.
asks: Is 'c' the same as total energy?
What is the difference between specific heat and heat?

faq.q: Do I need to use Joules or calories for the energy unit?
faq.a: In modern physics, Joules are the standard unit for energy. Always check which unit your question or textbook requires you to use.
asks: Can I use calories instead of Joules?
Which unit is best for this calculation?

faq.q: What does the 'ΔT' part mean in the calculation?
faq.a: Delta T, or ΔT, simply means the change in temperature. You calculate this by subtracting the starting temperature from the final temperature.
asks: How do I find the temperature change?
Is ΔT the final temperature minus the start?

faq.q: Does the specific heat capacity change if I mix two liquids?
faq.a: No, the specific heat capacity is a fixed property of the pure substance. Mixing them changes the total energy, but not the individual 'c' values.

faq.q: If I use grams instead of kilograms, how does the formula change?
faq.a: If you use grams for mass, you must use the corresponding units for energy and specific heat capacity to keep the equation balanced.
asks: What if I use grams for mass?
Do the units change if I use grams?

facts: The unit for specific heat capacity is Joules per kilogram per degree Celsius.
The formula used is Q equals mass times specific heat times change in temperature.
Water has a relatively high specific heat capacity compared to many other substances.
When calculating ΔT, always use the final temperature minus the initial temperature.

quiz.say: If you increase the mass of a substance while keeping the energy added constant, what happens to the temperature change?

options.show: The temperature change will stay the same.
options.say: The temperature change will stay the same.

quiz.why: Since mass is in the denominator when solving for ΔT, increasing mass lowers the resulting temperature change.

wrong.0: This suggests that more mass requires more energy to heat up.
wrong.1: This ignores the direct relationship between mass and temperature change.
wrong.2: The formula remains valid; only the result changes.

quiz.say: A substance has a specific heat capacity of 4200 Joules per kilogram per degree Celsius. If 2 kilograms of this substance cool down by 10 degrees Celsius, how much energy was lost?
quiz.why: You correctly used all three values: 4200 times 2 times 10 equals 84000.

wrong.0: This happens if you only multiply the specific heat by the temperature change.
wrong.1: This might result from incorrectly calculating the product of the mass and temperature change.
wrong.3: This mistake occurs if you forget to multiply by the mass of 2 kilograms.
